strengths: Addresses a useful problem: learning shared representations directly from NeRF weights across different architectures, enabling classification and cross-architecture retrieval.

The loss ablations provide convincing evidence that contrastive alignment improves cross-architecture retrieval. In Table 5, MLP-to-tri-plane recall@1 improves from 1.2% with rendering alone to 45.5% with contrastive training.
Single-architecture classification is competitive: 93.6% versus nf2vec’s 92.1%, and 94.0% versus Cardace et al.’s 93.1%. Generalization to several unseen depth and width variants also succeeds.
The paper clearly describes its framework and provides useful implementation details, dataset splits, training hyperparameters, and hardware costs.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: the parameter-graph construction and GMN encoder come from Lim et al., the decoder and rendering objective from nf2vec, and the contrastive objective from SigLIP. The contribution is primarily their application and integration, requiring stronger comparative evidence to establish significance.

The central multi-architecture experiments compare only the proposed loss variants. Architecture-specific encoders aligned with the same contrastive supervision would be an important baseline, alongside rendering-based representations. Marking existing methods as inapplicable does not establish that the proposed shared GMN is necessary or superior.

The claims of arbitrary-architecture robustness exceed the evidence. All experiments use one synthetic object dataset and two simplified, view-independent NeRF families; unseen architectures are size variations within these families. Table 3 also shows severe failures: with the classifier trained on BOTH, contrastive-only accuracy falls to 11.4% on TRI-8C, and the combined objective reaches only 21.3%.

Support for complete architecture invariance is insufficient. t-SNE overlap does not establish invariance, and substantial cross-architecture classification gaps remain. Retrieval on unseen architectures is not evaluated, despite unseen-architecture processing being a central contribution.

The evaluation lacks repeated runs or uncertainty estimates for the modest baseline improvements, tests of sensitivity to NeRF initialization and fitting quality, and quantitative reconstruction quality for the newly fitted architecture variants. These omissions make robustness and the causes of transfer failures difficult to assess.

Practical scalability is unresolved. Appendix D reports approximately two weeks of training for rendering-based variants, but inference latency, memory consumption, graph-size scaling, and comparisons against rendering-based pipelines are absent. Consequently, the practical efficiency motivation remains unverified.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful problem: learning shared representations directly from the weights of heterogeneous NeRF architectures.
Contrastive alignment produces substantial improvements over rendering-only training. Cross-architecture instance retrieval recall@1 increases from 1.2–2.7% to 44.1–45.5% (Table 5).
Single-architecture classification is competitive, achieving 93.6% versus nf2vec’s 92.1%, and 94.0% versus Cardace et al.’s 93.1% (Table 2).

The rendering-only, contrastive-only, and combined objectives provide useful evidence of a tradeoff between classification and architectural alignment. The appendix supplies substantial architecture and training details.
weaknesses: The methodological contribution is limited: the parameter graphs and GMN encoder are adopted from Lim et al., the decoder and rendering objective from nf2vec, and the alignment objective from SigLIP. The main novelty is their application and combination for NeRFs; stronger comparative evidence is needed to establish top-tier significance.

The central multi-architecture experiments compare only the proposed method’s loss variants. Marking existing methods as inapplicable does not replace competitive baselines, such as separate architecture-specific encoders trained with the same paired contrastive supervision, or rendered-view representations. Consequently, the benefit of a shared GMN over simpler alignment approaches remains unclear.

The 'arbitrary NeRF' and robust unseen-architecture claims exceed the evaluation. Both datasets represent the same synthetic ShapeNet objects, using two direction-independent architecture families. Unseen architectures are restricted to smaller variants of those families; no held-out architectural family, hash-grid NeRF, view-dependent representation, or real scene is evaluated.

Even these restricted architectural changes expose substantial failures. With the classifier trained on BOTH, TRI-8C accuracy is only 21.3% for the combined objective and 11.4% for contrastive-only training; rendering-only training reaches just 30.1% on TRI-16W (Table 3). These results distinguish accepting a graph input from learning a reliably architecture-invariant representation.

The alignment claim needs stronger qualification. Contrastive-only training lowers BOTH classification accuracy from 93.5% to 86.2%, while combined training achieves only 11.2% instance recall@1 in the mixed gallery. Qualitative t-SNE overlap does not establish complete architectural invariance, and unseen-architecture instance retrieval is not evaluated.

Evaluation lacks repeated-run uncertainty, sensitivity to the contrastive weight and batch size, and controls for the rendering quality of newly fitted NeRF variants. Efficiency is also unsubstantiated: training takes approximately two weeks for rendering-based variants, but inference latency, graph-construction cost, memory scaling, and comparisons with rendering-based pipelines are absent.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful limitation of existing NeRF weight-processing methods: learning a shared representation across different architectures.

Contrastive training substantially improves cross-architecture instance retrieval. In Table 5, MLP-to-tri-plane recall@1 increases from 1.2% with rendering-only training to 45.5% with contrastive-only training.
Single-architecture classification is competitive: 93.6% versus nf2vec's 92.1%, and 94.0% versus Cardace et al.'s 93.1%. Generalization to several unseen depth and width variants is also encouraging.
The manuscript is clearly organized, includes useful loss ablations, and provides dataset splits, architectural details, training hyperparameters, and hardware costs.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: the approach combines an existing GMN and graph construction, the nf2vec decoder, and the established SigLIP objective. Its main contribution is empirical, making the missing comparisons and limited generalization evidence particularly consequential.

The central multi-architecture experiments compare only loss variants of the proposed method. Architecture-specific encoders aligned using the same paired contrastive supervision would be an important baseline. A rendered-view baseline would also contextualize accuracy and practical efficiency.

The claim of robust handling of arbitrary or unseen architectures exceeds the evidence. Experiments cover two simplified, view-independent NeRF families on one synthetic object dataset; unseen architectures are size modifications within those families. In Table 3, reducing tri-plane channels yields only 21.3% accuracy for the combined objective and 11.4% for contrastive-only training, despite training the classifier on BOTH.

The combined objective has substantial unresolved tradeoffs. It reduces BOTH classification accuracy from 93.5% to 91.9% relative to rendering-only training, while its BOTH instance recall@1 is 11.2% versus 29.0% for contrastive-only training. No loss-weight sensitivity study establishes when the combined formulation is preferable.

Architectural compatibility is sometimes conflated with architecture-invariant representations. Reconstruction does not mathematically enforce nearby embeddings for similar objects, and t-SNE cannot establish invariance. The broad claim of being first to handle unseen architectures also needs qualification because Table 4 shows existing methods processing some unseen variants.

Evaluation lacks repeated runs or uncertainty estimates, reconstruction-quality controls for the newly trained NeRF variants, and inference-time or memory comparisons. These omissions limit confidence in the modest baseline improvements and leave the practical advantage unclear, especially given roughly two weeks of training for the rendering-based variants.

strengths: Addresses a relevant limitation of existing NeRF weight encoders: processing MLP, tri-plane, and hash-table representations with one shared encoder.
The proposed hash-table graph construction avoids explicitly expanding the underlying voxel grids, preserving their storage advantage.
Experiments cover three training architectures and ten unseen variants, with useful rendering-only, contrastive-only, and combined-loss ablations.
Contrastive training substantially improves cross-architecture instance retrieval: MLP-to-TRI Recall@1 increases from 1.8% to 30.6%, and TRI-to-MLP from 4.5% to 33.3%.

Single-architecture classification is competitive, improving over nf2vec from 92.1% to 93.6% and the tri-plane baseline from 93.1% to 94.0%. The appendix provides substantial architectural and optimization details.
weaknesses: The central multi-architecture experiments lack competitive external baselines. Listing architecture-specific methods as inapplicable does not establish superiority over separate encoders aligned using the same paired-object supervision, simpler parameter encoders, or rendered-view representations.

Methodological novelty is limited: the framework combines an existing GMN, the nf2vec decoder and rendering objective, and standard SigLIP alignment. The hash-table graph construction is a useful extension, but its particular design is not ablated against simpler alternatives.

Architecture independence remains substantially incomplete. With the classifier trained on ALL, the combined objective achieves only 30.8% on TRI-8C and 27.8% on HASH-11T. It also lowers classification accuracy on all three training architectures relative to rendering-only training. Mixed-gallery instance retrieval reaches only 5.3% Recall@1 and 27.2% Recall@10, indicating considerable residual architecture dependence.

Generalization evidence is narrow. All quantitative experiments use one synthetic object dataset and simplified, view-independent NeRFs; unseen architectures are smaller variants within known families. Objaverse evaluation is qualitative only, and the paper does not test larger networks, unseen families, or robustness across independent NeRF initializations.

The hash-table graph stores table and entry indices but does not explicitly encode the hashing function or grid-resolution schedule. The paper should clarify which architectural metadata must remain fixed and whether identical graph encodings can correspond to different spatial functions. Accepting variable graph sizes alone does not establish general architectural coverage.

Efficiency and reproducibility evidence is incomplete. Despite motivating weight processing as efficient, the paper reports no inference latency, peak memory, or comparison with rendering-based pipelines; training takes approximately two weeks on an A6000. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported, making the modest single-architecture gains difficult to assess, and the new NeRF datasets lack a fully specified fitting and quality-control protocol.

strengths: Addresses a relevant limitation of existing NeRF weight encoders: processing multiple architectures with one model. The compact hash-table graph construction provides a useful extension to existing graph meta-networks.

Evaluates three architecture families and ten unseen variants, with strong classification results on several depth and width changes. Single-architecture accuracy improves from 92.1% to 93.6% on MLPs and from 93.1% to 94.0% on tri-planes.
Includes rendering-only, contrastive-only, and combined-loss ablations. These demonstrate a meaningful tradeoff between class separation and cross-architecture alignment.
The appendices provide substantial architectural, optimization, dataset-split, and hardware details.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: the framework combines an existing GMN encoder, nf2vec decoder, and standard SigLIP objective. Beyond the hash-table graph construction, the paper does not establish a substantial technical advance over these components.

The central multi-architecture experiments lack competitive external baselines. Marking architecture-specific methods as inapplicable does not substitute for comparisons against separately trained encoders with learned alignment or rendering-based representations. Consequently, the practical advantage of the proposed approach remains unclear.

Architecture generalization is uneven. With encoder and classifier trained on ALL, the combined objective achieves only 27.8% on HASH-11T and 30.8% on TRI-8C (Table 4). Rendering-only training also fails badly on hash-table size and tri-plane resolution changes. These failures materially qualify the architecture-agnostic framing.

Cross-architecture alignment remains incomplete: combined-loss classification falls to 35.5% for HASH-to-TRI transfer, and instance retrieval on ALL/ALL achieves only 5.3% Recall@1 and 27.2% Recall@10. Large improvements over rendering-only training establish the usefulness of contrastive supervision, but do not establish strong absolute performance.

Quantitative evaluation is confined to one synthetic, object-centric dataset and simplified NeRFs without viewing-direction dependence. Objaverse evidence consists of selected retrieval examples. Robustness to independently initialized NeRFs, different fitting procedures, realistic scenes, and unseen architecture families is not established.

The hash-table representation records table and entry indices but does not explicitly encode the hashing function or spatial resolution schedule. The paper does not explain how it would distinguish fields with identical stored parameters but different spatial mappings, limiting the claimed generality of this representation.

No repeated-run uncertainty is reported for the relatively small gains over existing single-architecture methods. Inference latency, peak memory, and comparisons against rendering pipelines are also absent; the reported roughly two-week training time alone does not substantiate the efficiency motivation.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful limitation of existing NeRF weight encoders: handling multiple architectures with a shared representation. Supporting MLPs, tri-planes, and hash tables is a useful contribution.
The proposed hash-table graph construction preserves compact storage, with node and edge counts scaling with table size rather than the underlying voxel-grid resolution.

Experiments cover 13 architectures, including ten unseen variants. Performance is strong for several changes in MLP depth and width, and single-architecture classification improves over nf2vec and Cardace et al. by 1.5 and 0.9 percentage points, respectively.

Rendering-only, contrastive-only, and combined objectives are compared, including supplementary results. These experiments provide concrete evidence that contrastive alignment improves cross-architecture retrieval and that rendering supervision contributes useful semantic information.
The manuscript is clearly organized, and the appendix provides substantial architectural, optimization, dataset-split, and hardware details.
weaknesses: Comparative evaluation is insufficient for the central multi-architecture contribution. Tables largely compare loss variants of the same model; marking prior methods as inapplicable does not replace feasible baselines such as architecture-specific encoders aligned with the same paired supervision, or rendered-view embeddings. The practical advantage of the shared GMN remains incompletely established.

Architecture invariance is partial. With the classifier trained on ALL, the combined objective achieves only 30.8% on TRI-8C and 27.8% on HASH-11T (Table 4). Even among training architectures, HASH-to-TRI classifier transfer reaches only 35.5% (Table 2). These failures substantially qualify the broad robustness claims.

Instance retrieval remains weak in absolute terms: combined-loss Recall@1 is 5.3% for ALL/ALL and 9.5–33.3% for individual cross-family directions (Table 6). Improvements over rendering-only training are substantial, but qualitative similarity does not establish reliable instance alignment. Retrieval on unseen architectures is also not evaluated.

Methodological novelty is concentrated in the application and hash-table graph conversion: the encoder, decoder, and contrastive objective come from existing work. Stronger comparisons and analysis are needed to establish the significance of their combination, including sensitivity to loss weighting and the benefit of graph structure over simpler parameter encoders.

Generalization evidence is restricted to simplified, view-independent NeRFs of synthetic ShapeNet objects and architectural variants within known families. Objaverse evaluation consists of a few qualitative queries. Robustness to independently trained checkpoints, initialization changes, and broader hash configurations is not established.

The small single-architecture gains lack repeated-run uncertainty estimates. Although training takes approximately two weeks on an A6000, inference latency and memory comparisons are absent, leaving the efficiency motivation unverified. Overall, the promising contribution falls slightly below the acceptance threshold because its principal advantages need stronger comparative validation.
